title: Introduction to Geology
summary: Explore the structure of the Earth, plate tectonics, minerals and rocks, fossils and dating, natural resources, hazards and a geologist's field work and careers.
audience: Secondary and university students of geography, geology, mining and engineering

body.p: Geology is the study of the Earth: what it is made of, how it formed, and the processes that change it. The Earth has a radius of about 6,371 km. We cannot drill far, so scientists learn about the interior mainly from earthquake waves, which change speed and direction as they pass through different materials.

list: Crust: thin, solid outer layer, about 5 to 10 km thick under oceans and 30 to 70 km under continents.
Mantle: thick layer of hot rock reaching to about 2,900 km depth. It is solid but flows very slowly over long periods.
Outer core: liquid iron and nickel, from about 2,900 to 5,150 km depth. Movement here creates the magnetic field.
Inner core: solid iron and nickel, with a radius of about 1,220 km.

body.p: The lithosphere is the rigid crust plus the uppermost mantle. It is broken into plates that move on the softer asthenosphere beneath. The distance from the surface to the top of the core is about 2,890 km, so the core's own radius is about 6,371 - 2,890 = 3,480 km.

body.tip: Use a diagram when you revise. Draw each layer to scale and label state (solid or liquid) and main materials.

lessons.title: Plate tectonics: moving continents, earthquakes and volcanoes

body.p: The lithosphere is divided into about a dozen major plates and many smaller ones. They move a few centimetres a year, about the speed that fingernails grow. At 5 cm a year, a plate moves 500 km in 10 million years, which is enough to open an ocean over geological time.

list: Divergent: plates move apart. New crust forms, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the East African Rift.

Convergent: plates collide. An oceanic plate sinks under a continental plate (subduction) forming trenches, volcanoes and strong earthquakes. Two continental plates make fold mountains, as in the Himalayas.
Transform: plates slide past each other, as along the San Andreas Fault, causing earthquakes.
Matching coastlines and fossils on different continents.
Matching rock types and mountain belts across oceans.
The pattern of earthquakes and volcanoes along plate edges.

body.p: Earthquakes happen when stress that builds up in rocks is released suddenly along a fault. Magnitude is measured on logarithmic scales, so each step up means about 32 times more energy released. Preparation, such as strong buildings and drills, saves lives.

lessons.title: Minerals and the three rock families

body.p: A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure. Rocks are aggregates of one or more minerals. Geologists identify minerals by colour, streak (colour of the powder), lustre (how it shines), hardness, cleavage or fracture and density.

The Mohs scale ranks hardness from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond). Quartz is 7, calcite is 3, and fluorite is 4. A harder mineral scratches a softer one. A steel nail is about 5.5, so it scratches calcite but not quartz.

list: Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools. Intrusive rocks such as granite cool slowly underground and have large crystals. Extrusive rocks such as basalt cool fast at the surface and have small crystals.
Sedimentary rocks form when sediments are compacted and cemented, such as sandstone, limestone and shale. They often hold fossils and show layers.
Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change existing rock without melting it, such as marble from limestone and slate from shale.

body.p: The rock cycle links them: rocks can be weathered into sediment, buried, metamorphosed, melted and cooled again over millions of years.

The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. Geological time is divided into eons, eras and periods, such as the Cambrian, Jurassic and Quaternary. Most of Earth's history came before complex animals appeared.

list: Law of superposition: in undisturbed layers, the oldest are at the bottom.
Cross-cutting: a fault or intrusion is younger than the rocks it cuts.
Fossils: index fossils that lived briefly and widely help match layers in different places.

body.p: Some atoms are unstable and decay at a steady rate. Half-life is the time for half of the atoms to decay. If a sample starts with 100 g of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 10 million years, after 10 million years 50 g remains, after 20 million years 25 g, and after 30 million years 12.5 g. By measuring how much is left, scientists estimate the age of the rock.

body.tip: Fossils are most common in sedimentary rocks. Heat and pressure in metamorphic rocks usually destroy them.

body.p: Geology supports modern life. Metals such as iron, copper, bauxite for aluminium, gold, tin and coltan come from ores. Construction needs sand, gravel and limestone for cement. Energy comes from coal, oil, gas, uranium, and geothermal heat. Groundwater held in aquifers supplies wells and boreholes for millions of people.

body.p: Mining and drilling can damage land and water if poorly managed. Responsible geology includes environmental impact studies, rehabilitating land, fair treatment and safety for workers, and care for communities. Many countries are also looking for sources of minerals for batteries and clean energy, which brings both opportunity and responsibility.
Work safely in the field: wear a hard hat and boots, tell someone where you are going, check weather and hazards, and never undermine a cliff face.

Geologists collect evidence in the field. They observe rock outcrops, measure the angle of layers (dip) and direction (strike), sample rocks, record locations by GPS and draw sketches and cross-sections. A geological map uses colours and symbols to show rock types and structures across an area.

list: Hammer, hand lens and notebook.
Compass-clinometer for dip and strike.
GPS or phone map.
Sample bags and a marker.
Hard hat, gloves, goggles and first aid kit.

body.p: Geologists work in mining, oil and gas, groundwater and water supply, civil engineering, environmental consulting, geological surveys, universities and hazard monitoring. Most roles need a degree in geology or earth science. Some fieldwork roles train technicians. Rules for registration as a professional geologist differ by country.

body.tip: If you want to study geology, build strong foundations in maths, physics, chemistry and geography, and practise observing the rocks and landscape where you live.
